name: Name
title: Dragonfall
body: By Aeryn Rudel

name: Name
body:
The vault beneath Khardov stank of death. As Sabbreth walked through the dark labyrinth, her way lit by the demon glow of her warjacks’ blaze cores, she breathed the copper stench of fresh blood, but beneath that lingered the scent of bodies reduced to bone dust and scraps of rotting cloth.
The bleak stone halls were hauntingly familiar. They bore the leering faces and infernal scrawl of an Orgoth tomb, for long before the Immorese called this city Khardov, it had been Drak Galshogg, the greatest redoubt of Sabbreth’s people during the first invasion. Beneath it, they had interred their honored dead and hidden away their most blasphemous secrets. Secrets that would soon be hers.
Above, battle thundered, sending showers of dust down from the groaning stone roof. The majority of her forces fought in the city above. Horruskh led them, and though a victory in this place would further his glory, she only needed him to distract the Immorese while she plumbed the depths below the city for the true prize.

name: Name
body:
Ahead, through the narrow catacombs, the corridor opened into a wide hexagonal chamber, and the fine hairs on Sabbreth’s arms rose, and an electric thrill ran down her limbs. The presence of potent magic, ancient and terrible, lingered here. Her warjacks felt it, too, and one of her Jackals snarled, its bestial soul reacting to a magic not dissimilar to that which bound it inside its metal prison. She quieted the machine with a thought.
In the center of the chamber was a small stone platform, from which rose four basalt pillars, each the width of a large man’s arm and inscribed with spiraling infernal runes. From these four pillars hung chains of black iron, each terminating in a manacle currently locked around the wrists and ankles of a withered, mummified corpse. The chains seemed to be simultaneously suspending the body and pulling it apart. Though it was no doubt immensely heavy, two rotted wooden poles were inserted in the platform’s base so it could be carried.
Standing before the platform was a woman bearing the spear and shield of a senior warwitch. Therion Vhanek of the Path of the Reaper had removed her helm, letting her dark hair curl about her shoulders. The corpses of two Khadoran soldiers lay at Vhanek’s feet, their armor sundered by her spear, their blood staining her face. It made her all the more alluring. A dark angel drowned in crimson.

name: Name
body:
Sabbreth approached the warwitch and ran one hand lightly across her armored shoulder. A display of affection she would never indulge if they were not alone. Vhanek was her closest advisor, but she was more than that. She fulfilled both Sabbreth’s appetites for infernal knowledge, in which Vhanek was well versed, and her more carnal appetites, in which she was equally versed.
The ghost of a smile played across Vhanek’s mouth. "I have deciphered the script on the pillars."
"Is it the Lash?" Sabbreth breathed, unable to constrain the excitement in her voice. Khardov was an important strategic target, but what lay beneath the city, collecting dust since the first invasion, was far more valuable. It was the key to true conquest and a tantalizing piece of the prophecy that had drawn her across the ocean. The Lash of Horva was a weapon of such terrible might that the Orgoth opted to leave it behind when they left western Immoren centuries before. Fools, cowards, shortsighted and feeble. Those ancient warlords hadn’t the strength to wield it. She did.

name: Name
body:
"Half of it." Vhanek raised her blood-slicked spear, placed it beneath the bony chin of the bound corpse, and raised its head. Skeletal vertebrae cracked as the fleshless visage came into view. The bone structure was defined, noble, not unlike Vhanek’s. There was no denying the body bound to the dais was Orgoth. "The crown is missing."
Sabbreth reached out and ran her fingers along the weathered skull. There were marks in the bone, gouges in the temporal and occipital bone. Not quite deep enough to pierce into the brain cavity but no doubt excruciatingly painful.
"The crucible is useless without the crown," Sabbreth said, gritting her teeth. To be so close to her prize, only to have it be so far beyond her reach, was maddening. She felt the anger welling up inside her, her fractured soul—an imperfection from her last reincarnation—sending jagged shards of rage into her brain.
Her fingers curled around the hilts of her blades, her mind blazed into the souls of her warjacks, and the two Jackals began to stamp and scrape at the stone floor with taloned feet. She wanted to kill, to burn, to destroy. Anything to fill the gaping defect in her essence.

name: Name
body: "Sabbreth," Vhanek said softly. She removed her gauntlet and placed her hand at the juncture between Sabbreth’s gorget and helmet where a tiny sliver of her skin was exposed. The therion’s touch at first further enraged Sabbreth, then, as she moved closer, Vhanek’s words drew out the anger like poison from a wound. "All is not lost. Look there." Vhanek pointed with her spear to where a narrow passage led from the chamber. There were fresh footprints in the centuries of accumulated dust. Sabbreth pulled away from Vhanek, though not ungently. "Have any of our troops or theirs been here?" She nodded at the corpses of the Khadoran soldiers at his feet. "No. I opened the way, and left Reavers at the entrance. These made it past my guardians and followed me in. I killed them before they ventured further." A thunderous blast from above rocked the subterranean vault, and, worse, back the way Sabbreth had come, the red flow of a blaze furnace loomed and grew brighter. Horruskh. A few moments later, the Thousand Wraths entered the chamber like a conquering hero. He towered over both Vhanek and Sabbreth, his ornate armor scorched in places, gore-spattered in others. He carried his great sword over his shoulder as if the massive abyssal blade weighed nothing. Behind him, one of his warjacks, a particularly fearsome Tyrant called Molok, growled and hissed.

name: Name
body: "You found it," Horruskh said, grinning hugely beneath his helm. The man possessed an infuriating joviality that scratched at Sabbreth’s every nerve. He was skilled, ancient, blessed by the Fellgoeth, yet he seemed to find humor in everything. "You doubted?" Sabbreth said. "Of course not," Horruskh replied, chuckling. "I was the one who put it here so no one would be tempted to use it. I thought poor Lorgoth here was the last to be so foolish." He pointed at the desiccated corpse bound to the crucible. His eyes twinkled. "I was wrong." She ignored the barb and flung one of her own. "How goes the battle?" The smile fell away from his face. "They have . . . unexpected allies. We are pulling back." "Oh? Have you lost the city? You assured me it would fall." "We have lost nothing," Horruskh said. "We could take Khardov, but it would expend too many resources." "Resources?" Sabbreth laughed. "The great Horruskh the Thousand Wraths now counts soldiers and barrels of grain instead of the souls of the damned?"

name: Name
body: "Someone must," Horruskh said. His smile remained, but it had soured. "While you chase prophecy and ancient weapons, Kishtaar and I lead us to victory." "Prophecy is why we are here," Vhanek said. "Prophecy is why you are here." Sabbreth did not disagree with the therion, but Dagholoth’s prophecy could be painstakingly detailed and maddeningly vague at the same time. The prophet had written specifically about the Lash of Horva, a weapon more ancient than even he, and that it was needed to overthrow the Immorese gods, but he hadn’t mentioned why or how it was to be used. She had taken it as a good omen that Horruskh had known about the Lash and where to find it, but he remained as doubtful of the prophecy as ever and would tell her little more about the artifact than she’d already gleaned from Dagholoth’s cryptic writings. Horruskh glared at Vhanek, and his Tyrant Molok took a step toward the therion, hissing like a great serpent. "Perhaps so, Therion, but to seek the Lash of Horva is to invite destruction."

name: Name
body: "I invite only the destruction of our enemies," Sabbreth cut in. "Lorgoth the Harbinger thought much the same," Horruskh said, again indicating the withered corpse. "He thought the Lash would grant us victory four hundred years ago, and he lost everything to it. His life, his soul, even his line was ended." "I am not him," Sabbreth said. "You are not," Horruskh said grudgingly. "Perhaps you are stronger than Lorgoth, or perhaps I will also bury you in some darkened tomb when the Lash destroys your mind." Sabbreth turned away, back to the footsteps in the dust. Horruskh’s words had unnerved her, as was no doubt his intention, and for that slight, she would repay in kind. "How long before you lose control of the city?" The momentary silence before Horruskh spoke pleased Sabbreth immensely. "In one hour, we are relocating to the coast to reassess our advantage." "I will join you there," Sabbreth said. "Vhanek, with me." She started down the corridor, following the footsteps. They were humanoid, some booted, some massive and barefooted. Behind her, the blazing light of Horruskh’s Tyrant faded, but his words remained. Perhaps I will bury you. She pushed them away. She would not allow the warlord to sow doubt and cloud her purpose.

name: Name
body:
The corridor made a sharp right turn and then ended abruptly in a blank stone wall. The flooring had been torn up; bare dirt was exposed beneath it. It reminded Sabbreth of the small burrowing mammals that infested the highlands of Drak Orgoroth.
A body lay in front of the sundered floor, human but strangely altered. Its hands had been removed and replaced with mechanikal prosthetics—a crude drill and a rotating saw. It wore a heavy bronze helmet bolted onto a metal collar, and the rest of its body was clothed in tattered rags. It had been killed by half a dozen arrows or darts that protruded from its neck and chest. They were of ancient Orgoth make, and Sabbreth also noted the six holes on the far wall at head and chest level.
"Do you recognize this being?" she asked Vhanek. The warwitch was highly knowledgeable about western Immoren and had been in regular contact with the spies they’d sent in before the invasion.
"A cephalyx drudge," Vhanek said, kneeling in front of the corpse. "It hasn’t been dead long. A day at most."

name: Name
body: Sabbreth knew little of the cephalyx beyond the fact they were subterranean and were given to mental powers and "improving" their servants with radical surgery. "Why would they take the crown?" "Perhaps they didn’t know what it was?" Vhanek said. "Or perhaps they did," Sabbreth replied. The vault shook again as the battle in the city raged or perhaps reached a crescendo as Horruskh left their foes a parting shot. "I want the crucible removed and brought with us." "I will see it done," Vhanek said. "We will find the crown." Sabbreth nodded. "Even if I have to dig up half the continent to root it out."

name: Name
body: Kommander Valerii Savaryn watched from the ramparts of Khardov’s battlements as the Orgoth host withdrew, an armada of warships choking the Lothpool River and sailing south toward the Blackroot Wood. Calling it a retreat would be overstating the situation, as would calling what had happened today a victory for Khador. They had been on the brink of destruction, the city within moments of being overrun, when a call for aid sent out weeks before, to ally and former enemy alike, had been answered. The first to arrive at their beleaguered city had not been any of the great nations of western Immoren. Not any of the great human nations, anyway, Savaryn thought. He looked down to the southern gates, where a small force of their saviors’ troops and warjacks guarded the entrance to the city. The myrmidons of House Kallyss differed from those he had seen in the past. They were lithe and effective fighting machines powered by ineffable and ancient arcane technology, just as any Iosan warjack was, but they glowed with a strange amber radiance that Savaryn found mildly disconcerting. Strangely, their jagged swords and barbed flails reminded him of sharpened fangs.

name: Name
body: "Sir?" a voice behind Savaryn said. He turned to see his adjutant, Lieutenant Boris Ovcharka, a gray-haired lifer who’d started in the Winter Guard twenty years earlier and transitioned into the Winter Korps. Ovcharka’s right arm was bound in a sling—he’d taken an Orgoth harpoon. The grizzled veteran hadn’t bothered to pull it out until after he’d split the skull of the warrior who’d fired it. "One of the, uh, commanders of the Iosan forces wants to speak with you." "Me?" Savaryn said. "About what?" He’d fought alongside their newest allies, but he was hardly a diplomat. In fact, his commanding officers often made sure he was not put into such situations. He had a bad habit of asking blunt questions when subtle words were needed. He assumed diplomatic matters would be left to Posadnik Tishnikov and Kommandant Makarov, who oversaw the city’s defenses. "Apparently, he’s found something," Ovcharka said. "Kommandant Makarov would like you to investigate." Savaryn had been fighting nonstop for three days, and though weariness gnawed at his limbs and the inside of his warcaster armor stank with a rancid mingling of coal and sweat, the prospect of speaking to of the bizarre leaders of House Kallyss filled his mind with questions. Questions, more than anything, drove Valerii Savaryn. The drive for knowledge, to learn, had pushed him into the Druzhina at the age of fifteen when his warcaster talent had awakened, and it had led him to victories on the battlefield where he asked, How can this foe be beaten? and then relentlessly acquired the knowledge to do so.

name: Name
body:
Questions, more than Makarov’s order, propelled him now. "Take me to him."
#
The streets of Khardov were choked with corpses and the wreckage of fighting machines. Orgoth warriors and Winter Korps soldiers lay in gruesome heaps, and in some places, the bodies were so mangled it was impossible to tell which was which. Savaryn had seen battle in all its terrible forms since he’d left the Druzhina, first in Llael against Cygnar, then in countless border skirmishes, and more recently, in the horrific war against the infernals. Still, the abject savagery with which the Orgoth conducted war had taken him by surprise. They were fearless, without mercy, and utterly brutal.
Lieutenant Ovcharka led him to Khardov’s industrial district, to the base of the great basalt fortress that had belonged to the Orgoth during their initial invasion that then became a stronghold for the Greylord Covenant. The black walls towered, sheer and malignant, a cancerous stain against a bloody sky.
"There, sir," Ovcharka said and pointed to where a group of myrmidons and House Kallyss soldiers gathered near a gaping hole in the wall of the fortress. The hole was new, and Valerii Savaryn could see it led to a subterranean corridor that angled down sharply. Dozens of tombs and vaults had been discovered beneath Khardov over the centuries. Many held ancient weapons and terrible magics the Greylords had used to increase their power, power that had eventually led them to betray the Motherland.

name: Name
body:
Valerii approached the waiting Iosans, wishing he’d brought a warjack with him, but he was loath to remove any of their fighting machines from the battlements lest the Orgoth return. Even in his bulky warcaster armor, he felt small and insignificant.
He passed through the ranks of Iosan soldiers, who silently parted to let him through. Like the myrmidons, these soldiers and their jagged weapons and armor exuded a subtle menace. Their arms and equipment were alien, but, worse, they were frighteningly still and disconcertingly silent.
The one who had summoned him stepped forward. The Iosan’s warcaster armor was dotted with nodes of amber luminescence and was considerably less bulky than Valerii’s own armor. Strange projections jutted from the Iosan’s pauldrons, reminding Valerii of fingers. No, not fingers. Legs. Insectile legs. The Iosan wore no helm, and his angular face was pale and gaunt, the lips a bloodless gray, eyes like miniature yellow suns blaring from sunken sockets. A shock of thick white hair rose in an impressive topknot from the Iosan’s head, bound by a silver crown or diadem.

name: Name
body: "Kommander . . . Valerii . . . Savaryn?" the Iosan said, his voice a strained whisper. It was as if the words simply emanated from the warcaster rather than were spoken by him. "I am . . . Tyrus, Nis-Arsyr of Spiders." Valerii had some understanding of Iosan titles, and a Nis-Arsyr was a high-ranking noble or religious title. The epithet "of spiders" was a mystery, though oddly fitting for this strange being. "You asked to speak with me," Valerii said. "Why?" "I am told you are a learned man," Tyrus said. The rhythm of his words was becoming more natural, as if he had suddenly remembered how to supply breath and voice to them. "That you have studied the Orgoth extensively." When the Orgoth had returned, Valerii Savaryn had spent every moment not fighting them by delving into the history of the first occupation, records of battles, obscure lore compiled by the Greylords, all in hopes of learning how best to fight them. "I am a student of our enemy, yes." "I, too, have been fascinated by them," Tyrus said. Valerii would have preferred a different word than fascinated, but he was still intrigued. "I believe they came to Khardov for a very specific purpose."

name: Name
body:
"Beyond destroying us?"
Tyrus nodded his pale head. "Do you notice? There are no bodies, no wreckage, and little damage in this place."
Valerii glanced around and saw what the Iosan said was true. There was little evidence of fighting beyond a few Winter Korps corpses directly outside the hole in the fortress wall. "You’re right. Why?"
"I will show you. Follow me below."
#
The glow from their respective warcaster armors provided some light in the darkened catacombs below the great fortress, but Valerii took with him a lantern to guide their way just the same. He wasn’t sure if Tyrus even needed light to see in the dark, but the Iosan made no complaint.
"See these markings?" Tyrus said, stopping where the corridor widened a bit. He ran a bony-fingered hand over a leering face, its eyes wide, its mouth open in a silent scream. Below the face were a pair of crossed blades. "I’ve seen this in other tombs. There is or was more here than honored dead."
Valerii pointed his lantern at the floor. "Look at the tracks. These are fresh. They brought warjacks with them as well." The Orgoth machines were bestial things, and the tracks they left looked more like some great predatory beast than any warjack.

name: Name
body:
"But so few," Tyrus said. "While their forces attacked from the river to the west, drawing your defenses there, one of their warlords came here, opened this vault, and removed something."
There were two Orgoth warlords they knew of, warcasters and sorcerers of incredible power. Their names were unknown to him, but Valerii had seen the towering hulk of a man armed with a massive sword and clad in ornate armor during the battle. The woman Kapitan Borisyuk had defeated near Skrovenberg had not been seen during the battle. "Removed what?"
"I will show you this as well," Tyrus said.
They traveled farther into the vault, and Valerii made note of the runes scrawled on the walls. Most were simple evocations to the infernals the Orgoth served. Like the prayer tapestries that hung in a Morrowan church, more a show of devotion than any kind of active magic. A large chamber opened ahead, its floor coated with dust, where two Winter Korps corpses lay in patches of dried blood.
Something large had been dragged away, and it had left a swath of cleared dust back the way they had come.

name: Name
body:
"Whatever they came for was here," Tyrus said.
"And now they have it," Savaryn said. "This vault was undiscovered. There are no records of what it might have contained."
"It is a weapon. It could be naught else," Tyrus said.
"You don’t think the attack on Khardov was just to allow them access to this vault?" Sevaryn said. "A ruse?"
"Not entirely. I believed their purpose was divided." Tyrus knelt and ran a finger through the dust and blood on the floor. "Divided and at least partially successful."

name: Name
body:
The castle had been called Rastok before Sabbreth and Horruskh had razed the woods around it, slaughtered its defenders, and made it a temporary redoubt for attacks farther inland. Its proximity to the river called the Lothpool allowed them to offload troops and warjacks with lightning speed or to gather reinforcements from strongholds they’d established nearer the coast. Now, they returned to Rastok with a heavy burden. They had not been defeated at Khardov, but neither had they been victorious, which meant they had taken few prisoners.
"How many?" Sabbreth asked. She was seated on the throne-like chair in the castle’s great hall. It was the only piece of furniture in the cavernous space. All but she would stand, even Horruskh, even the warwitches who had informed her that their tithe to the Fellgoeth was expected. Souls for their dark masters normally drawn from the thousands of prisoners they took from each sacked city, each village burned and looted.
"Not enough," Horruskh said. "A few hundred."

name: Name
body:
He did not smile. He did not joke. The joviality he had shown back in Khardov had withered and died. If proper sacrifices were not made to the Fellgoeth, then their continued immortality, their very existence, was at risk. Sabbreth and Horruskh disagreed on nearly every aspect of the campaign, but in this, they were united. Eternal destruction had a way of bringing even the most bitter rivals together.
"There must be a culling," Therion Vhanek said, her voice grave. She stood among the warwitches gathered in a semicircle around Sabbreth’s makeshift throne; most were therions or stygians of the Path of the Reaper or Shadows, respectively. As a Matron Tenebrous of the Path of the Reaper, Sabbreth outranked them all, but her responsibilities did not allow for a regular commune with the Fellgoeth as those with more singular duties.
Sabbreth nodded. "What do the Fellgoeth demand?"
"Five hundred and twelve," Therion Vhanek said.
Horruskh drew in a deep breath and let it out slowly, likely as close to a gasp as the warlord would allow himself. "We have half that in prisoners from Khardov and elsewhere."

name: Name
body: "Then we must gather the rest from the reaves." Sabbreth stood and pointed one finger at the assembled warwitches. "Only the strong and hale. We can ill afford to be miserly." "I took one of their battle sorcerers, their warcasters. Only an apprentice but valuable," Horruskh said. "I had thought to question her or hand her over to the Vulcar, but . . ." Doom unites, Sabbreth thought to herself. "Yes, it will sweeten the offer." She turned to the assembled warwitches. "Dig the pit. I will make the offering myself." # The offering began at dawn the next day. The blood pit had been dug in the ground before the castle. Braziers spewing rancid smoke surrounded it, and a dozen warwitches swayed at its perimeter, their voices lifted in a guttural chant. Sabbreth sat cross-legged at the bottom of the pit, looking up through the smoke, letting the warwitches’ voices pour over her. She had stripped down to her small clothes—there could be no barrier between her flesh and the offering—and she gripped a long, wavy-bladed knife in her right hand.

name: Name
body: "Are you ready, Matron?" Vhanek said from the edge of the pit. Screams and cries of horror joined the warwitches’ chanting, and Sabbreth nodded. "By the blood of the weak are we made strong." "By the souls of the unworthy is the dark held at bay," Vhanek said, then turned and shouted, "Bring forth the first." A pair of nocturnes, one each from The Path of the Reaper and the Path of Shadows, appeared at the edge of the pit. Between them was a young man, stripped to the waist, his chest thin and fish-belly white from lack of food and long imprisonment. His eyes were twin moons of horror in his gaunt face, and his mouth hung open, a line of spittle dangling from his bottom lip. He was terrified beyond rational thought. Good, Sabbreth thought. Terror should open the way. The nocturne of the Path of the Reaper produced a curved knife from beneath her robes, set the point at the base of the prisoner’s breastbone—he did not struggle but merely glanced down at the blade with a kind of dazed curiosity. The nocturne rammed her knife into the prisoner’s flesh. He gasped and then loosed a long syrupy grunt as the nocturne ripped the blade down through his abdomen. Blood gushed, spattering Sabbreth’s face with warmth, and the prisoner’s intestines unspooled from his torn belly like a nest of pink eels.

name: Name
body:
The nocturne made more cuts, and more pieces of the prisoner fell into the pit—most importantly, his heart. She was quick and efficient, and soon the first offering had no more to give. His limp body was carried away. It would be burned, an empty vessel fit only for annihilation.
What followed was a blur of screams and pleas for mercy. The pit began to fill with blood and viscera, and soon Sabbreth’s legs and hips were submerged in the precious effluvia. Its warmth was calming, its odor alluring, and she began her own chant, quickening the organic mass with infernal magic.
The next set of offerings were drawn from their own number. Some had volunteered, and they went first, making the initial cut with the sacrificial knife using their own hands. The nocturnes took over when their strength faded. The rest had to be restrained, and Horruskh and Vhanek took over the sacred duties of harvesting their flesh.
The sun set, the pit filled, and Sabbreth stood chest deep in the thickening mass. Her prayers to the Fellgoeth grew louder and joined the ululating cries of the warwitches above. She held her own ceremonial blade aloft, and now the final sacrifice was led to the edge of the pit.

name: Name
body: She was tall, muscular, and her face was set in stony defiance. Even when she saw Sabbreth, a blood-drenched demon howling from the bottom of a pit of human offal, her face did not change, fear did not claim her. Her hands were bound behind her back, and she wore her warcaster armor—though it was not powered up. Horruskh stood behind the woman and he spoke in passable Khadoran. "What is your name?" In response, the woman turned and spat full in the warlord’s face. He took a step back, grinning, holding up a hand to keep his more loyal soldiers from slaughtering the woman. "I am Lieutenant Irena Vaskovich, dog. I am a child of the Motherland, a servant of Menoth, and the only thing you can take from me is my life." Not the only thing, Sabbreth thought. Bravery was good. The ritual must start with fear and end with defiance. The Fellgoeth enjoyed all flavors of human suffering. Horruskh approached the Khadoran warcaster, still grinning. "Would that we could cross blades once more," he said then lashed out with a booted foot and kicked her into the pit. She fell with a muffled curse, hitting the slowly coagulating offal with a splash and disappearing beneath it.

name: Name
body:
Sabbreth was on top of her in an instant. She drove one hand beneath the gore, grasped the woman’s armor, and pulled her gasping to the surface. Now, finally, fear overcame her, and she opened her mouth to scream. Sabbreth did not let her—she cut the woman’s throat from ear to ear, letting the breath and life leak from her body.
The Khadoran warcaster sank beneath the surface, and Sabbreth chanted the final words of the ritual, feeling power swell beneath her.
There was one more sacrifice to make. Sabbreth reversed her grip on the knife, leveled it at her breast, and drove it home. The world disappeared, and the offering was considered.
#
Sabbreth floated in the darkness, unmoored from reality or substance. She had visited the lightless halls of the Fellgoeth many times, and each time, she had been assured of returning from them. Now, she doubted, and that doubt led to fear.
She crushed that fear and waited. The Fellgoeth would accept the offer or she would remain here, unbodied, for eternity.

name: Name
body:
An emotion washed over her suddenly. Satisfaction. Appeasement. The Fellgoeth rarely spoke in their own halls. They communicated more cryptically, and they still had much to show her.
The darkness fell away, and Sabbreth saw a volcano rising from a range of mountains, a single towering spike of rock and flame. The top of the volcano smoked then glowed with a rancid green light, a hellish gleam that Sabbreth knew represented a terrible power, one nearly equal to the Fellgoeth themselves.
Suddenly, the mountain erupted, spewing fire and geysers of magma across the plains below. Something massive and terrible stirred within this destruction. It burst from the volcano and spread wings large enough to blot out the sun. The dragon reared up, and Sabbreth recoiled in terror at its otherworldly power, but then it loosed a long, lingering screech of rage as great chains appeared from nowhere and lashed its wings and limbs tightly to its body. The bound dragon was lifted up, exposing its chest, and Sabbreth’s vision pierced the scales and alien flesh to the great glowing gem beneath. The athanc. The heart of a dragon.

name: Name
body: The vision changed abruptly from the erupting volcano to a storm-tossed sea. From out that sea rose a great island dotted with spires of black basalt and granite. It reminded her of Drak Orgoroth, but it was an imitation. No, not an imitation—a perversion, and a powerful one. Return. Return. Return. The single word echoed in Sabbreth’s mind as the vision fell away, and the harsh light of reality crashed in. # Sabbreth awoke on her sleeping palate in the room she had claimed for herself in the castle. She lay on her back, her body washed clean of blood and gore. She clutched at her chest where she had plunged the ceremonial knife. There was no wound, no pain. The Fellgoeth had accepted her offer. They had accepted her offer and then shown her a path to further glory, to the fulfillment of the prophecy she had followed across the sea. She now understood why she needed the Lash of Horva. She needed it to kill a dragon.
